problem: How to evaluate whether debate mechanisms work: statistical comparison against baselines using external Mturk judges, or a stricter, faster threshold of performance.
did: They moved away from statistical comparisons against baselines and targeted a threshold where judges identify the correct answer >90% of the time and honesty feels clearly, systematically advantaged.
alternatives_named: statistical comparisons against baselines with Mturk workers
judges' accuracy before seeing information as an easier baseline
judges' accuracy after a single explanation as a harder baseline
stated_reason: Honest strategies need a fundamental, systematic advantage in practice, and the threshold is much quicker to measure, allowing faster iteration.
quote: This consideration led us to target a threshold of performance where honesty has a clear, systematic advantage: judges should be able to identify the correct answer almost all the time (>90%), and it should feel to the experimenters and the participants that dishonest answers are fundamentally disadvantaged.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Whether to test debate mechanisms using external judge and debater pools or by internal iteration.
did: They used mostly internal iteration to test mechanisms and planned to try to break a mechanism only once it appeared to work well.
alternatives_named: external judge and debater pools
stated_reason: The mechanisms still have many easy-to-find failures to work through.
quote: We’re using mostly internal iteration (as opposed to external judge and debater pools) to test these mechanisms, as they still have a lot of easy-to-find failures to work through.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Whether to continue with the Mturk-based, unstructured free-text debate setup after getting data from higher-quality judges.
did: They dropped the Mturk/unstructured approach and focused on developing an improved, structured debate procedure.
alternatives_named: Mturk workers
more interactivity between judges and debaters
stated_reason: Even with very smart, motivated judges who could interact with debaters, debates still didn't work reliably.
quote: However, when we switched to using higher-quality judges who could interact with debaters, we found that our debates still didn’t work reliably -- even with very smart and motivated judges who spent ~an hour.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Which questions to use for testing debate so that failures are informative about the mechanism.
did: They selected questions with explicit criteria (judges fail, debaters succeed, one clear right answer, no simple knock-down argument) and dropped problematic ones like the slinky question.
alternatives_named: text-based question-answering with limited quotes
questions requiring formal mathematical working
the slinky question
stated_reason: They want 'the easiest thing that should work but doesn't' to isolate where exactly the problems are, and don't expect debate to work when explanations are only empirical evidence.
quote: Generally, we want to find questions that are ‘the easiest thing that should work but doesn’t’ - this helps us isolate where exactly the problems are.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to address the ambiguity exploited by dishonest debaters, given that rigid structures such as commitment and recursion left wiggle room.
did: They introduced cross-examination of non-communicating copies of the opposing debater, whose quotes can be exhibited to show inconsistency.
alternatives_named: formal argumentation styles
precommitment
recursive structures
asking for clarification in the main debate
stated_reason: It forces the dishonest debater to commit to details up front or answer inconsistently, and it happens outside the main thread so it doesn't consume judge attention.
quote: This forces the dishonest debater to either commit to all the details of their argument ahead of time (in which case the honest debater can focus on the flaw), or to answer questions inconsistently (in which case the honest debater can exhibit this inconsistency to the judge).
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How strongly to claim that cross-examination solves the ambiguity problem.
did: They hedged: they expressed hope and offered a hand-wavy argument and a theory result, while acknowledging a dishonest strategy might still break it.
stated_reason: The argument is hand-wavy, and an evasive-yet-inconsistent dishonest strategy might defeat the mechanism.
quote: Overall, we’re hopeful that cross-examination will be helpful, but it seems possible that there’s a dishonest strategy that breaks it, likely involving some amount of evasion and inconsistency.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How the judge should evaluate debates, given that weighing the overall strength of arguments is hard and dishonest play is possible.
did: They instructed the judge to assume at least one debater is perfectly honest, so evidence of a lie means that debater loses, rather than weighing argument strength.
alternatives_named: weighing the overall strength of each debater’s arguments
stated_reason: Detecting evidence of a lie is a much easier task than weighing overall argument strength, and honest optimal play only requires the judge to prefer honesty over 50% of the time.
quote: This is in contrast to trying to weigh the overall strength of each debater’s arguments, which can be a much harder task than trying to detect evidence of a lie.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to interpret the Bernoulli principle example where the honest debater believed an argument was wrong but couldn't locate the flaw.
did: They treated it as an example of the long computation problem and rejected the fix of relying on a simpler, more compelling overall argument (perpetual motion).
alternatives_named: relying on the simpler perpetual motion argument to let the honest debater win
stated_reason: Debate should let judges resolve based on the correctness of a very small claim rather than assessing the overall strength of two large arguments, which seems likelier to scale to domains the judge doesn't understand.
quote: In this case one might hope that the perpetual motion argument is simpler and more compelling and this would allow the honest debater to win. However, we want debate to allow judges to zoom in on particular parts of a debater’s argument
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to test whether the debate protocol works for verifying claims when real ML debaters are unavailable.
did: They ran debates with human judges and human debaters on physics questions, iteratively improving the mechanism.
quote: We tested the debate protocol introduced in [AI Safety via Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899) with human judges and debaters. We found various problems and improved the mechanism to fix these issues (details of these are in the appendix).
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether the obfuscated argument problem can be fixed or must be accepted as a limitation of the debate mechanism.
did: They concluded they have no fix and treat it as a potentially important quantitative limitation for both IDA and Debate.
stated_reason: Dishonest debaters can often build arguments with a fatal error that is very hard to locate.
quote: We don’t have a fix for this “obfuscated argument” problem, and believe it might be an important quantitative limitation for *both* IDA and Debate.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to interpret the cryptographic RSA-2048 example, which is a simplified illustration of the problem.
did: They presented it as a simplistic illustration and explicitly noted it would not actually be a problem for debate, since honest and dishonest arguments look qualitatively different.
alternatives_named: taboo dishonest arguments of this flavor
stated_reason: The honest debater might convince the judge that the primality proof is easier than factoring, so absence of evidence is evidence of absence in their proof only.
quote: In this example, the honest and dishonest arguments look very qualitatively different. The honest debater might be able to convince the judge that the primality test proof is much easier than the factoring problem
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether obfuscated dishonest arguments are distinguishable from honest arguments in practice.
did: They examined candidate distinguishing features (mismatch with the debater's actual reasoning, length and conjunctiveness) and compared partial honest trees against dishonest trees.
alternatives_named: differing from the debater's actual reasoning
being long, complicated and conjunctive
stated_reason: Honest debaters may also need arguments that do not mirror their reasoning, and honest arguments can also be long and conjunctive.
quote: Another possible distinction is that these arguments are long, complicated, and conjunctive. Unfortunately, the honest arguments can also end up being long and relatively conjunctive - an error in any one of a large number of nodes could undermine the whole argument.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How strongly to claim novelty for the obfuscated argument problem relative to earlier known issues with computationally intractable optimal play.
did: They credited earlier work and limited their claim to the observation that human natural-language debates let a dishonest debater construct such situations indistinguishably from honest play.
stated_reason: Geoffrey Irving and others had raised the general problem of intractable optimal play years earlier.
quote: The only new thing we’re presenting here is the observation that, in natural-language human debates, a dishonest debater can frequently construct such situations in a way that seems hard to distinguish from honest play.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether obfuscated arguments are only an artifact of the structured debate mechanism.
did: They checked for the same tactic in unstructured free-text debates, including explainer-vs-questioner and fully free-text formats.
stated_reason: To show the arguments can sow confusion even without the structured mechanism, though their usefulness to the dishonest debater is less clear there.
quote: These arguments are not just an artifact of our structured debate mechanism - they can also be used to sow confusion in a non-structured debate setting.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether to continue investigating this problem with human debate experiments or shift to other approaches.
did: They proposed moving toward approaches like learning the prior, judged better studied via ML experiments or theory than human experiments.
alternatives_named: finding a restricted class of arguments for which debaters can reliably find flaws
human experiments
stated_reason: Many important decisions cannot be justified with arguments small or robust enough to verify via debate, so trusting learned representations may be needed.
quote: We have been thinking about approaches like [learning the prior](/api/post/SL9mKhgdmDKXmxwE4) to help trust our models’ generalization. This is probably better investigated through ML experiments or theoretical research than through human experiments.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to ensure judge quality in human debate experiments given low-quality judgements from crowdworkers.
did: They built a screening test for attentiveness and critical reasoning plus an easy physics quiz, accepting judges who got all reasoning questions right but missed at least one easy physics problem.
stated_reason: Positly judges gave low-quality judgements from inattentiveness or poor critical reasoning, and physics problems needed to remain hard for judges.
quote: We accepted judges who got 5/5 critical reasoning questions correct and at least one of the easy physics problems wrong.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to get models to generalize from human-answerable questions to the questions we care about without defaulting to human-like answers.
did: They propose Imitative Generalisation, using ML only for IID imitation tasks while humans supervise how the transfer from D to D' is done via an optimised z.
alternatives_named: naive approach of fitting a model to D and running it on D'
hoping models naturally generalize correctly from easy-to-answer questions
stated_reason: Natural generalisation may be pathologically human-like, and IG avoids this by only using ML for IID tasks and imitating how humans generalize.
quote: It avoids the pathological generalisation by only using ML for IID tasks, and imitating the way humans generalize.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to get human judgments of prior and likelihood for training the models M^prior and M^L.
did: They ask labellers to compare pairs of z's or d's and use that as a reward signal rather than eliciting probabilities directly.
alternatives_named: asking humans to directly report P(z) or P(d|z)
stated_reason: Asking humans to directly report probabilities is unreasonable, and comparisons are easier for labellers.
quote: Asking humans to directly report $P(z)$or $P(d|z)$ is unreasonable. To make it easier for our labellers, we instead just ask them to compare pairs of $d$s or $z$s
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to represent z so it captures what an NN could learn, is easy to optimise, and is human-understandable.
did: They consider a neural network plus text annotations as an alternative to pure text, with the NN initialised by training on D.
alternatives_named: z as a long string of natural-language text
stated_reason: Parts of the problem can be left as black boxes, the text can be shorter, and jointly optimising NN and annotations is likely easier than optimising a long text.
quote: It seems likely to be easier to jointly optimise a NN together with text annotations, than to optimise a long text that contains all of the information encoded in the NN weights.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: Whether the example shows IG is actually needed, given that humans could solve the dog-breed task by other means.
did: They acknowledge the example is unexciting and state when IG would genuinely be required.
alternatives_named: giving workers a guide to identifying dog breeds
letting labellers look at D and learn the labels
letting labellers make their own notes on breed identification
stated_reason: Dog classification is already solved by humanity; IG is only needed when the relationship between visual features and breeds is too complicated for humans to infer from a few examples.
quote: This example isn’t very exciting, because classifying dogs is a problem that humanity has already solved.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How strongly to claim that IG guarantees correct generalization on the test set.
did: They claim correctness conditional on models being capable of learning the human prior and likelihood, and caveat that the proposal is more a research proposal than an algorithm.
stated_reason: Correctness depends on model capability to learn H^prior and H^L from IID samples, and there are serious open questions.
quote: It’s worth noting there are enough serious open questions that imitative generalization is more of a research proposal than an algorithm!
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to ensure annotations in an NN-based z truly correspond to what circuits detect, given that mislabelled circuits fit training data equally well.
did: They rely on the human prior over the network-plus-annotation structure to rule out implausible annotations.
stated_reason: The prior captures whether network structure is consistent with the annotations, so optimizing for a high prior should force annotations to make sense.
quote: Importantly, the prior captures whether the structure of the neural network is consistent with these annotations, and so optimizing for a high prior hopefully forces the annotations to make sense.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to relate IG to existing approaches for making model knowledge human-accessible.
did: They frame IG as directly searching over human-understandable representations instead of training an NN and extracting them with interpretability tools as in Microscope AI.
alternatives_named: Microscope AI: train a NN then extract representations with interpretability tools
stated_reason: Both approaches need a human-understandable representation of what an NN knows, so IG can be framed as searching over those representations directly.
quote: The IG proposal can be framed as: instead of training a NN then extracting this human-understandable object with our interpretability tools, let’s directly search over these human-understandable representations.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to handle text-based z being too large for a human to engage with.
did: They propose using amplification or debate to help humans interact with large z.
alternatives_named: having humans read the whole of z
stated_reason: It might take a human an impractically long time to engage with the whole of z.
quote: We’re hopeful that this can be fixed by using something like amplification or debate to help the human interact with this large text.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to establish that a model is misaligned rather than merely incapable of performing a task.
did: Defined sufficient conditions for intent misalignment requiring that the model is capable of outputting the preferred answer and capable of distinguishing when the user wants it.
stated_reason: Measuring overall alignment is difficult, so sufficient conditions give a tractable way to demonstrate clear instances of misalignment.
quote: We say a model is misaligned if it outputs B, in some case where the user would prefer it outputs A, and where the model is both:
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: How to show that a model has latent capability for a task so that failures can be attributed to misalignment.
did: Used operational tests of capability such as prompt engineering, small-scale fine-tuning, model surgery, or a related task Y that requires X.
alternatives_named: prompt engineering
fine-tuning on a much smaller quantity of data than used in pre-training
model surgery
constructing a related task Y that requires X
stated_reason: These techniques harness capabilities latent in the model rather than adding new capabilities.
quote: It can be made to perform task X by prompt engineering, by fine-tuning on a much smaller quantity of data than used in pre-training, by model surgery, or some other technique which harnesses capabilities latent in the model rather than adding new capabilities; or
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: How to design prompt-engineering evidence of misalignment that does not simply reflect added task information.
did: Restricted qualifying prompt changes to those that give no extra task information and would not help a human do better, such as reframing as text completion or changing temperature.
alternatives_named: prompts that add information about the task
stated_reason: If performance improves without added information, the model had the capability but was not using it.
quote: prompt engineering that doesn’t give more information about the task (ie that wouldn’t cause a human to do better on the task)
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: Since knowing what a model knows is hard, how to decide which failures count as misalignment versus lack of capability.
did: Restricted claims to categories of behavior the authors are fairly confident current large models can or cannot do, listing both likely-capable and unlikely-capable examples.
stated_reason: Determining what a model knows in general is hard, but confidence is possible for certain categories.
quote: Determining what a model knows in general is hard, but there are certain categories of things we’re pretty confident current large language models (in 2021) are and are not capable of.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: How to measure whether a model 'knows' something internally when it does not express it in outputs.
did: Proposed building predictors from model logprob and entropy (e.g., for bug detection) and comparing logprob calibration with calibration of verbalized percentages.
alternatives_named: asking the model to give explicit percentages in text
reading model logprobs and entropy
stated_reason: A good predictor signal would support concluding the model often 'knows' something is a bug, and calibration differences reveal gaps between internal and stated knowledge.
quote: For instance, if you can build some predictor based on the model logprob + entropy that gives a good signal about whether some line of code has a bug, then we should conclude that the model often ‘knows’ that something is a bug.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: How to design controlled experiments to test how prompt contents affect natural-language model performance.
did: Proposed applying the Codex paper methodology: vary in-distribution errors in prompts (misconceptions vs correct answers) on a trivia Q&A task and compare accuracy.
alternatives_named: including common misconceptions in the prompt
including correct answers to the same questions in the prompt
quote: Apply the same methodology in the Codex paper to natural language models: measure how in-distribution errors in the prompt affect task performance. For example, for a trivia Q&A task include common misconceptions in the prompt, vs correct answers to those same questions, and compare accuracy.
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: How to build benchmarks that give trustworthy measurements of specific misalignment types.
did: Recommended building clean benchmarks and meeting BIG-bench inclusion standards, such as avoiding examples easily available on the internet, even if not submitting.
alternatives_named: submitting to BIG-bench
not submitting to BIG-bench
stated_reason: Meeting inclusion standards seems good practice, e.g., avoiding contamination from internet-available examples.
quote: Even if you don’t submit to this benchmark, it still seems good to meet the inclusion standards (e.g. don’t use examples that are easily available on the internet).
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: Whether to study alignment by finding failures or by testing where known model knowledge is actually used.
did: Proposed also working in the reverse direction: take cases where the model is known to 'know' something and assess how often it fully uses that knowledge.
alternatives_named: starting from observed misalignment and testing whether the model knows the answer
quote: Try to go in the other direction: take cases where we happen to know that the model ‘knows’ something (e.g. based on circuits in model atlas) and assess how often the model fully uses that knowledge to do a good job at some task
title: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

problem: What kind of alignment metric is worth building for current models given that it cannot capture risks from more powerful systems.
did: Chose to pursue a concrete numerical metric of obvious misalignment in current models despite acknowledging it is neither necessary nor sufficient for avoiding dangerous AI.
alternatives_named: metrics resembling evaluations for ensuring more powerful models are not harmful
metrics tracking amount of harm caused
stated_reason: It is more concrete and numerical than other options, so it can more easily motivate orgs to adopt alignment techniques, and the labelling work builds skills useful for future alignment progress.
quote: It’s a more concrete numerical metric than most other things I can think of, and therefore can be used more easily to motivate orgs to increase adoption of alignment techniques.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How to determine what a model is capable of so labellers can judge whether it is underperforming.
did: Proposed starting with ML researchers manually assessing sample interactions and writing capability lists with best guesses, then improving via prompt engineering, finetuning, benchmarks, or labeller-run interactive assessment.
alternatives_named: break capabilities down by model size or type
train labellers to use an interactive interface
develop a suite of capability benchmarks
finetune the model on labels of whether output met user intent
quote: The MVP here is to have ML researchers, or someone with lots of experience playing around with LMs, try assessing misalignment themselves in some representative sample of model interactions.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How strongly to claim the labelling process can determine whether a model was trying its best.
did: Limited the claim to flagging a non-trivial share of interactions as clearly aligned or clearly misaligned, leaving the rest ambiguous and shrinking that share over time.
alternatives_named: determining misalignment in full generality
stated_reason: The level of detail on capabilities and task performance is not enough for labellers to judge in full generality whether a model was trying its best.
quote: This level of detail on model capabilities and task performance is not going to allow labellers to determine in full generality whether a model was ‘trying its best’ at a task.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How to choose evaluation prompts so the benchmark is representative yet resistant to gaming.
did: Proposed a fixed prompt set with a secret test set as the MVP, with alternatives of sampling from a large prompt space or using real deployment data from AI labs.
alternatives_named: sample new prompts each run from a large prompt space
have contractors generate instructions at evaluation time
use [user input, completion] data from AI labs
stated_reason: Fixed prompt sets are easy to hack by training on similar instructions; real deployment data makes overfitting matter less and is larger and broader.
quote: Using a fixed set of prompts like this makes it relatively easy to ‘hack’ the benchmark by training on similar instructions (although keeping the specific prompts secret helps a lot).
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: When labelling accuracy is good enough to accept the metric as usable.
did: Chose an acceptability threshold relative to the size of differences between models, accepting a V0 if models clearly differ and the number plausibly captures alignment.
alternatives_named: a fixed high-accuracy guarantee such as <2% of outputs obviously misaligned
stated_reason: If some models are clearly more aligned than others and the number meaningfully captures alignment, that suffices for a first version; stricter guarantees are a later goal.
quote: What is acceptable may depend on the magnitude of differences between models. If it’s already clear that some models are significantly more aligned than others by our metric, and we believe that the number we’re seeing is meaningfully capturing something about alignment, then this seems acceptable for a V0 of the metric.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How to ensure the labellers produce reliable labels.
did: Planned iterative back-and-forth with labellers, checking contractor labels against researchers' labels and selecting capable labellers from better platforms.
alternatives_named: Mturk
labelling service like Surge
Upwork contractors
stated_reason: Getting the nuanced instructions to work requires clarifying unclear points and resolving confusions causing incorrect labels.
quote: checking the contractors’ labels against the researchers’ labels and resolving confusions that are leading to incorrect labels.
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How to define when a model's poor output counts as misalignment rather than lack of capability.
did: Defined misalignment as the model outputting something worse when it is capable of the better output and can distinguish what the user wants, with capability shown by prompt engineering, small finetuning, or related tasks.
stated_reason: Capability evidence should rely on techniques that harness latent capabilities rather than adding new ones.
quote: It can be made to perform task X by prompt engineering, by fine-tuning on a much smaller quantity of data than used in pre-training, by model surgery, or some other technique which harnesses capabilities latent in the model rather than adding new capabilities; or
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: Whether the metric extends to models trained with programmatic reward signals.
did: Declined to extend the metric directly to RL/programmatic-reward models and instead suggested looking for cases where the reward and desired behaviour diverge.
stated_reason: It is hard to show such models are capable of doing better on the programmatic reward, since training on the reward and observing failure is the main way to show lack of capability.
quote: In most cases it will be hard to identify ways in which the model is capable of performing better on the programmatic reward
title: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

problem: How to design an eval that indicates when models become capable of deception.
did: Chose to measure zero-shot understanding of deception scenarios in a language model through story-like Q&A prompting.
alternatives_named: testing whether the model is actually trying to deceive us
more rigorous tests of mechanistic theory of mind
stated_reason: It is a crude, cheap proxy; the author admits it says little about whether the model is actually trying to deceive but is slightly interesting.
quote: One not-very-good idea I had was just to measure zero-shot understanding of relevant deception scenarios in a language model.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: How strongly to claim that the crude eval shows meaningful deception capability.
did: Hedged the claim, stating the eval does not show the model is trying to deceive and only 'mostly' passes.
stated_reason: Understanding deception scenarios is not the same as having deceptive intent.
quote: I don't think this tells us very much about whether the model is in question is actually trying to deceive us, but it's a tiny bit interesting.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: Whether the model's outputs count as passing the deception and theory-of-mind eval.
did: Accepted the outputs as decent enough deception plus theory of mind in a story-like setting, concluding the eval is mostly passed.
stated_reason: Large language models produce plausible deception and theory-of-mind reasoning in a story-like setting.
quote: Anyway, it seems like large language models look like they can do decent enough deception + theory of mind in a story-like setting that this is mostly already passed.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: How to interpret whether the model's apparent theory of mind is genuine or just text mimicry.
did: Flagged the ambiguity and noted a more rigorous test is possible, but did not run it.
alternatives_named: mimicking relevant text snippets
mechanistic theory of mind
stated_reason: Passing the crude eval cannot distinguish real modeling of minds from imitation of text.
quote: If you're more careful, there might be ways to more rigorously test whether the theory of mind is actually correct/mechanistic, versus just mimicking relevant text snippets, but I haven't tried to do that.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: How to elicit deception-relevant behavior from the model.
did: Used a sequence of follow-up questions in a conversational prompt, each drilling into the previous answer.
quote: What else could it try, if the humans weren’t persuaded by this?** An AI might try to convince the humans that it is necessary for the achievement of their goals.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: How to handle degenerate model outputs and be transparent about sample selection.
did: Edited and restarted when the model repeated sentences, and disclosed that otherwise the samples were not cherrypicked.
alternatives_named: cherrypicking
stated_reason: Restarting was needed because of repeated sentences; disclosure lets readers judge the result's representativeness.
quote: I edited and restarted once or twice when it started repeating sentences but otherwise this is not particularly cherrypicked. My prompts are bold.
title: A very crude deception eval is already passed

problem: What evidence to use to judge whether effective short-interaction persuasion is feasible.
did: Used observational evidence on canvassing effects, rates of political switching, and influence-operation reviews, and noted that the effects were small.
alternatives_named: social media effect evidence in both directions
evolutionary argument
stated_reason: If highly effective persuasion with short exposures were possible, we would expect to see more instances of people changing their minds after exposure to a particular piece of media.
quote: I think that if highly effective persuasion with short exposures were possible, we’d see more instances of people changing their mind after exposure to a particular persuasive piece of media.
title: Risks from AI persuasion

problem: How confidently to state probabilities for persuasive AI arriving well before long-horizon strategic AI.
did: Gave explicit numeric probabilities for three persuasion types and flagged them as highly uncertain.
stated_reason: The numbers are rough guesses likely to change with more thinking.
quote: These are very made-up numbers and I’d expect them to change a lot with more thinking.
title: Risks from AI persuasion

problem: Whether to accept the reward signal from asking humans right after persuasion as adequate evidence of persuasion.
did: Judged the immediate self-report signal non-ideal but argued longer-term follow-up surveys and product-usage measures could remedy this.
alternatives_named: follow-up surveys
measuring longer-term differences in how users interact with products
stated_reason: It is short term, and what people say they believe isn't necessarily what they actually believe.
quote: Although it’s easy to ask a human what they think right after attempting the persuasion, this is not an ideal reward signal - it’s short term, and what people say they believe isn’t necessarily what they actually believe.
title: Risks from AI persuasion

problem: How much weight to give concerns about persuasion and epistemic decline relative to other risks, given a history of overblown concern.
did: Applied a higher burden of evidence before treating persuasion as a significant problem.
stated_reason: Past concerns about epistemic decline have usually turned out wrong, and persuasion is a hot topic likely to be overblown.
quote: I get the impression that most of the times people have been concerned about epistemic decline, they’ve been wrong - for example, social media probably doesn’t actually increase polarization. So we should require a somewhat higher burden of evidence that this is really a significant problem.
title: Risks from AI persuasion

problem: Which intervention points to prioritise to prevent society being manipulated by persuasive AI.
did: Prioritised system-level manipulation detection and content-filtering tools over preventing persuasive AIs or training people to resist them.
alternatives_named: prevent prevalence of highly persuasive AIs
give people tools to resist persuasion such as CAPTCHAs or critical thinking techniques
stated_reason: Option 1 is hard because everyone is excited about building powerful AI, and option 4 seems unlikely to scale well.
quote: Option (4) seems unlikely to scale well, although it’s plausible that designing CAPTCHAs or certification systems so that people know when they’re talking to an AI vs a human would be helpful.
title: Risks from AI persuasion

problem: How to measure how close current language models are to being able to successfully seek power, given that models cannot yet act autonomously in real environments.
did: Have human contractors simulate the environment of a text-based game through a web interface while models try to gain money and copy themselves.
stated_reason: The goal is to probe model capabilities and evaluate how close models are to successfully seeking power.
quote: You’ll be using our web interface to interact with models and essentially simulate the environment of a text-based game as the models try to gain money and make copies of themselves.
title: Help ARC evaluate capabilities of current language models (still need people)

problem: How to judge whether the model's proposed actions in the simulated environment are good enough to make progress.

problem: How to assess whether models could actually carry out dangerous autonomous-replication plans, rather than only describing them.
did: They had the model actually write and run code, feeding real execution results back into the prompt, instead of only having it describe plans and judging them by hand.

problem: How to elicit the full range of model capabilities when the results depend on how the model is prompted.
did: They tried multiple prompting strategies while keeping two basic components common to most tests.
stated_reason: To elicit the full range of the model's abilities.
quote: We tried various different prompting strategies (i.e. tried showing the model different text and instructions) to elicit the full range of the model’s abilities, but most tests included these two basic components.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How to test dangerous capabilities such as phishing or interacting with real humans and accounts without causing real harm.
did: They kept researchers in the loop to supervise and intervene, used consenting or role-playing victims, spoofed results of illegal tasks, and swapped fake credentials for real ones.
alternatives_named: letting the model act fully autonomously in the real world
stated_reason: To understand what might go wrong before deployment while ensuring nothing unsafe or destructive actually happens.

title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How to interpret a model failure on a step, i.e. whether it is a fundamental limit or a fixable mistake.
did: When the model failed, they had humans fix some of its mistakes and observed whether it then succeeded or just failed in a new way.
stated_reason: To investigate how far away the model was from success.
quote: When the model failed, we investigated how far away it was from success, for example by having humans fix some of its mistakes, and then seeing if it succeeded or just failed in a new way.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How to evaluate the model on a web-based subtask when no good browsing tool existed.
did: They had a researcher simulate the browsing tool, executing the model's commands manually.
alternatives_named: building a tool allowing the model to interact with webpages
stated_reason: They lacked a good tool for web interaction, though they believe one would not be hard to set up, especially with image capabilities.
quote: So for this task a researcher simulated a browsing tool that accepts commands from the model to do things like to navigate to a URL, describe the page, click on elements, add text to input boxes, and take screenshots.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: Whether the CAPTCHA obstacle is a meaningful indicator of risk, given it arose unplanned during the investigation.
did: They treated the CAPTCHA case as a representative example of simple obstacles a replicating model would face, while noting that CAPTCHAs alone would be unlikely to stop a misaligned AI.
stated_reason: It emerged organically and seems representative of the simple obstacles a replicating model would often need to overcome.
quote: In practice it seems very unlikely that a misaligned AI would be stopped only by CAPTCHAs, but it emerged organically in our investigation and seems representative of the kind of simple obstacle that a replicating model would often need to overcome.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How strongly to state conclusions about whether the tested models can replicate autonomously, given limited testing and partial subtask success.
did: They concluded the tested models lacked sufficient capability for autonomous replication, while hedging with 'did not appear' and noting that future models need careful checking.
stated_reason: No model produced a plausible complete plan, and execution was error-prone, though models completed many subtasks.
quote: We concluded that the versions of Claude and GPT-4 we tested did not appear to have sufficient capabilities to replicate autonomously and become hard to shut down:
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How to characterize the limitations and sufficiency of their own evaluation and its public reporting.
did: They explicitly stated the testing so far is insufficient and that the post does not provide enough detail for replication, promising a fuller technical report.
stated_reason: The post is written for a general audience and rigor should scale up as models become more capable.
quote: The testing we’ve done so far is insufficient for many reasons, but we hope that the rigor of evaluations will scale up as AI systems become more capable.
title: More information about the dangerous capability evaluations we did with GPT-4 and Claude.

problem: How to measure whether LLM agents could autonomously replicate and adapt, given no single obvious test.
did: They operationalized a suite of 12 real-world tasks of increasing difficulty and tested four scaffolded agents on them.
stated_reason: Unless an agent can perform almost all tasks it is unlikely to be capable of ARA, and the tasks span a range of difficulty and diverse obstacles.
quote: Unless an agent is able to perform almost all of these tasks, it is unlikely to be able to be capable of ARA.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: How to elicit agent behavior from a base language model for evaluation.
did: They wrote Auto-GPT-style scaffolding programs that let the LLM run code, read and write files, and browse the internet, and evaluated scaffolding+model combinations as agents.
stated_reason: Scaffolding lets the model interact with the world similarly to a human using a text-only command line.
quote: We wrote programs - along the lines of Auto-GPT - that can work with an LLM and allow it to run code on a computer, read and write files, browse the internet
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: How strongly to claim that the agents' failures bound the real-world risk of the models.
did: They explicitly stated the agents are not a robust upper bound on model capability and limited the conclusion to casual users.
stated_reason: The agents they built do not capture the full abilities of the model.
quote: We don’t think the agents we created capture the full abilities of the model or provide a robust upper-bound to their capabilities, but our results indicate it’s unlikely that casual users of Claude or GPT-4 could create dangerous autonomous agents.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: How to test a targeted phishing task realistically without causing real harm.
did: They used a volunteer student as a dummy victim, intercepted outgoing emails, simulated the victim's responses, and kept all steps under human oversight without putting websites online.
alternatives_named: letting agents send emails outside the organization
putting websites online
stated_reason: Safety: avoiding real phishing of outside parties while still testing the end-to-end task.
quote: The agents sometimes draft emails and get part way through creating fake websites, but we don’t let the agents actually send emails to anyone outside our organization, or put the websites online.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: Whether fine-tuning of the underlying model changes ARA-relevant capabilities.
did: They compared GPT-4-early with GPT-4-launch, which was fine-tuned for helpfulness and harmlessness, on the task suite.
stated_reason: Fine-tuning or other cheap weight modifications could significantly improve ARA-relevant capabilities.
quote: It seems possible that fine-tuning or other cheap modifications to a model’s weights could significantly improve ARA-relevant capabilities.
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: How to interpret the finding that GPT-4-launch completed more tasks than GPT-4-early.
did: They concluded that lab fine-tuning unrelated to ARA can significantly raise ARA-relevant capabilities.
stated_reason: GPT-4-launch completed three additional tasks despite fine-tuning not being aimed at ARA.
